item.title: Lettonie La " Liste unie" du Premier ministre largement en tête des élections
item.description: La " Liste unie", formation centriste et pro-ukrainienne du Premier ministre letton Andris Kulbergs, semble en passe de signer une plus large victoire que prévu au scrutin législatif organisé samedi, les électeurs ayant ainsi exprimé leur inquiétude par rapport à une possible agression russe.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: La " Liste unie", formation centriste et pro-ukrainienne du Premier ministre letton Andris Kulbergs, semble en passe de signer une plus large victoire que prévu au scrutin législatif organisé samedi, les électeurs ayant ainsi exprimé leur inquiétude par rapport à une possible agression russe. Le sondage à la sortie des urnes réalisé par la chaîne publique lettone LSM montre ainsi que la "Liste unie" a remporté 35,6% des voix, devant le parti populiste "Lettonie d’abord", qui s'inspire du mouvement "Maga" du président américain Donald Trump, avec 11,3% des suffrages. "Lettonie d'abord" avait notamment courtisé l'importante minorité ethnique russe de la Lettonie à l'approche du scrutin. Vers la mi-juillet, les présidents lituanien et letton, Gitanas Nauseda et Edgars Rinkevics, ont [USN:L8N43H0SI TEXT:"accusé"] la Russie de projets de sabotage contre des pays de l'Otan, accusations qualifiées par Moscou de "fables alarmistes". Au début de même mois, la Pologne avait dit que les services de renseignement occidentaux s'inquiétaient du risque d'attaques russes contre son territoire et les États baltes. Moscou dément régulièrement ce type d'accusations qui s'inscrivent selon elles dans le cadre d'une campagne de propagande antirusse. Il y a quelques jours, l'Estonie a dit être parvenue à la conclusion qu'un [USN:L8N45L0XL TEXT:"incendie"] ayant eu lieu en août dans les locaux de la société de défense Milrem Robotics, fournisseur de drones terrestres pour l'Ukraine, était un acte criminel commandité par les services de sécurité russes. NÉCESSITÉ DE TROUVER UN ALLIÉ POUR GOUVERNER Réagissant aux résultats des sondages à la sortie des urnes, Andris Kulbergs a déclaré qu’il espérait rester Premier ministre, ajoutant qu'il ne souhaitait pas gouverner avec "Lettonie d'abord". Si les sondages à la sortie des urnes sont confirmés par les résultats officiels, le Premier ministre aura besoin d'alliés pour être en mesure de former un gouvernement. "C'est remarquablement bon. Je ne m'attendais pas à un tel résultat", s'est félicité Andeis Kulbergs au siège de son parti à Riga. Le parti des Progressistes arrive en troisième position dans le classement des sondages à la sortie des urnes, avec également 11,3%, suivi du parti ouvertement pro-russe "Sovereign Power", avec 10,8%. Outre les questions de sécurité, celle du coût de la vie a également dominé la campagne électorale en Lettonie, État membre de l'Otan et de l'Union européenne qui partage une frontière avec la Russie et abrite une importante minorité russophone. Andris Kulbergs, homme d’affaires et pilote de rallye amateur de 47 ans, est arrivé au pouvoir en mai après l'effondrement de la [USN:L6N41R0M0 TEXT:"coalition précédente"], en raison de la façon dont cette dernière avait géré des incidents au cours desquels des drones militaires avaient pénétré dans l'espace aérien letton sans être détectés. Tout au long de sa campagne, il a promis de renforcer les capacités anti-drones de la Lettonie et de maintenir les dépenses de défense à 5% du produit intérieur brut, l'un des niveaux les plus élevés de l'OTAN. La Lettonie, qui compte 1,9 million d'habitants, longe la mer Baltique, avec au nord et au sud l'Estonie et la Lituanie, alliées de l'UE et de l'Otan, et à l'est la Russie et la Biélorussie.

item.title: Fernandes rejects talk of Portugal rift after Ronaldo's abrupt departure
item.description: Bruno Fernandes said on Saturday he had spoken to Cristiano Ronaldo and dismissed suggestions of a rift within Portugal's squad after the captain's abrupt departure from the national team's training camp cast doubt over his international future.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Bruno Fernandes said on Saturday he had spoken to Cristiano Ronaldo and dismissed suggestions of a rift within Portugal's squad after the captain's [USN:L6N45M17Z TEXT:"abrupt departure"] from the national team's training camp cast doubt over his international future. Portugal's record goalscorer Ronaldo, 41, left the camp in Copenhagen on Wednesday shortly after coach Jorge Jesus acknowledged tensions between the pair. The Al-Nassr forward departed a day before Portugal's Nations League group-stage clash with Denmark, a match Jesus' side went on to win 4-2. Ronaldo said on Instagram that he made the decision after Jesus' news conference and a conversation with Portuguese Football Federation President Pedro Proenca, adding that he would reveal his reasons "in due course". "I had a chat with him and what I said to him is what I'll repeat here: the most important thing is that, whatever happens, Cristiano Ronaldo will never cease to be the greatest symbol of our national team, of our football and of the country," Fernandes told a news conference ahead of Sunday's Nations League match against Norway in Porto. "For what he has achieved not only in Portugal, but all over the world. He has a place reserved not only amongst the all-time greats, but also in the hearts of all Portuguese people. "The most important thing is that we stop stirring up trouble; there are no divisions within the national team. It is one team and will remain so, despite any noise that may come from outside." Spanish newspaper Marca reported that Portugal manager Jorge Jesus and Portuguese Football Federation President Pedro Proenca made an [USN:L6N45N0IW TEXT:"unsuccessful dash"] to Copenhagen airport in an attempt to persuade Ronaldo not to leave the squad. "The most important thing is that this ends well, for both sides," the 32-year-old Manchester United captain added. "We're completely out of the picture; we're aware of what you're saying and what we're seeing. We've spent a lot of time in the players' room playing cards; we're on the sidelines of this controversy, but what I ask is that the country doesn't become divided, doesn't take sides, and respects all parties..." Jesus, meanwhile, sought to shift the focus back to Norway. Portugal top Group A4 on nine points from three matches, with Norway third on three. "The focus has to be on the national team, the match against Norway, and what we need to do well, in tune with our people," he said. "But that doesn't mean I'm ignoring Cris. He's a symbol of the Portuguese national team; he's a symbol of Portugal - let that be quite clear. "After the match, there'll be time to talk about that."

item.title: OpenAI safety employee quits, says 'time for trial and error is over'
item.description: A former OpenAI safety employee who recently resigned criticized the company's approach to AI safety, arguing that a fast-paced culture focused on rapid development increases the risk of failures.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: A former OpenAI safety employee who recently resigned criticized the company's approach to AI safety, arguing that a fast-paced culture focused on rapid development increases the risk of failures. Writing in "I Quit OpenAI Because Its Culture Is Broken," published by the Atlantic on Saturday, David Robinson said AI companies, including OpenAI, were not being "nearly careful enough" and should place greater emphasis on safety expertise and research before developing more capable systems. "The time for trial and error is over," Robinson wrote, arguing that advanced AI systems require safeguards more akin to those used in industries such as nuclear power and aviation. Robinson said OpenAI relies heavily on what it calls "iterative deployment," releasing systems and strengthening safeguards when problems emerge. The comments add to a [USN:L6N45L0PN TEXT:"debate within the AI industry"] over whether companies are moving too quickly to develop increasingly powerful systems. [USN:L4N45L05X TEXT:"OpenAI"] and rival [USN:L6N45L00I TEXT:"Anthropic"] have faced scrutiny after incidents in which safety controls failed, or experimental systems behaved unexpectedly. Robinson, who said he spent 3-1/2 years at OpenAI, helped draft the company's preparedness framework and oversaw safety reports for 12 frontier-model launches, wrote: "As the company sprints from one launch to the next, it is failing to achieve the level of care that I believe is needed." "We're making sure our models don't become more capable than we can safely manage and secure, and we pause training or hold back models when we need to slow down," an OpenAI spokesperson said in a statement. Robinson also warned that AI capabilities were advancing faster than researchers' understanding of alignment, a field focused on ensuring AI systems act in accordance with human goals and values.

item.title: England crush Croatia 7-0 as Spain stay perfect with Czech victory
item.description: Harry Kane and Bukayo Saka scored twice apiece as England demolished Luka Modric's Croatia 7-0 in Rijeka on Saturday, but Spain stayed three points clear at the top of their Nations League group with a 3-1 victory over the Czech Republic.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Harry Kane and Bukayo Saka scored twice apiece as England demolished Luka Modric's Croatia 7-0 in Rijeka on Saturday, but Spain stayed three points clear at the top of their Nations League group with a 3-1 victory over the Czech Republic. Jude Bellingham scored once and provided three assists for England, with Anthony Gordon and substitute Morgan Rogers also on target in a performance captain Kane described as "unbelievable". England are second in League A, Group Three with six points from three matches, behind Spain on nine. Croatia have three points and the Czechs remain pointless. "Unbelievable from start to finish," Kane told ITV. "We spoke a lot about having a 90-minute game from start to finish, being completely dominant with the ball and without the ball. That was it right there." Kane took his international tally to 89 goals in 124 appearances, moving within one cap of Peter Shilton's England record. Asked about potentially drawing level with Shilton against the Czech Republic on Tuesday, Kane said: "Would be nice. That is why he (manager Thomas Tuchel) takes me off, to save me for the next one!" England went ahead after little more than seven minutes when Josko Gvardiol lost possession and Bellingham released Kane, who slipped between two defenders and fired home. Bellingham doubled the lead in the 21st minute after Gordon turned Saka's cross back across goal. Gordon added the third in the 39th, meeting Jarell Quansah's cross with a first-time finish. Mateo Kovacic squandered a close-range chance before Bellingham crossed for an unmarked Saka to score a minute before halftime. Elliot Anderson supplied Kane's second goal with a low cross in the 53rd minute, before Josip Stanisic's misplaced pass across his own box gifted Saka another goal in the 68th. Bellingham released Rogers to complete the rout three minutes from time. "They couldn't live with our pace, with our runs," Kane said. SPAIN KEEP WINNING World and European champions Spain maintained their perfect start in Oviedo despite coach Luis de la Fuente making nine changes to the side that beat Croatia 4-1 on Tuesday. Lamine Yamal opened the scoring in the sixth minute, curling a stunning left-footed shot into the top corner from the edge of the box. After Spain squandered several opportunities, captain Rodri doubled their advantage by converting a rebound inside the area, his first international goal in more than two years. Jiri Slama gave the visitors hope in the 69th minute, finishing a swift counter-attack with an angled shot just inside David Raya's right post. Their chances of an equaliser faded when Ladislav Krejci received a second booking in the 85th minute for holding back an opponent to stop a counter-attack. Mikel Merino then sealed Spain's victory, finishing first time from inside the box following another quick break. In League B, Scotland won 2-0 at North Macedonia through goals from Kieron Bowie and John McGinn before Scott McKenna was sent off in the 83rd minute. Switzerland came from behind to beat Slovenia 2-1 in Luzern, with an Erik Janza own goal and Dan Ndoye's strike overturning Zan Vipotnik's opener. The Swiss lead Group One on nine points, with Scotland and Slovenia level on four.

item.title: L'Ukraine va intensifier ses frappes sur les raffineries russes
item.description: L'Ukraine va intensifier ses attaques contre les raffineries russes en réponse à la nouvelle stratégie de frappes aériennes menée par Moscou visant à forcer la population à quitter Kyiv et d'autres villes, sans pour autant prendre pour cible les civils, a déclaré le président ukrainien Volodimir Zelensky.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Flynn, Olena Harmash
item.content:encoded: L'Ukraine va intensifier ses attaques contre les raffineries russes en réponse à la nouvelle stratégie de frappes aériennes menée par Moscou visant à forcer la population à [USN:L8N45P02B TEXT:"quitter Kyiv"] et d'autres villes, sans pour autant prendre pour cible les civils, a déclaré le président ukrainien Volodimir Zelensky. Les services de renseignement ukrainiens ont obtenu des documents montrant que le président russe Vladimir Poutine a défini une "nouvelle doctrine" prévoyant des attaques militaires contre un éventail beaucoup plus large de cibles civiles à l'approche de l'hiver, a déclaré Volodimir Zelensky. "Nous avons vu ces documents et nous savons qu'ils leur permettent d'attaquer les infrastructures (...) la logistique (...) les routes, les écoles, les hôpitaux, afin de faire pression sur la population pour qu'elle quitte la capitale et d'autres villes", a-t-il ajouté. D'après la président ukrainien, ce changement de doctrine s'explique par la volonté de Vladimir Poutine de faire une démonstration de force à un moment où son armée perd du terrain sur le front et subit des pertes de plus en plus importantes. Le Kremlin n'était pas disponible samedi pour commenter ces informations. Mais le ministère des Affaires étrangères russe a déclaré plus tôt dans la journée que la Russie continuerait à mener des frappes sur Kyiv et d'autres villes ukrainiennes, exhortant les ressortissants étrangers et les diplomates à quitter la capitale ukrainienne. Les deux parties nient prendre délibérément pour cible des civils. CONTRE-OFFENSIVE DANS LE DONBASS Selon Volodimir Zelensky, une contre-offensive ukrainienne en cours, baptisée "Vivaldi", a permis de reprendre environ 140 kilomètres carrés dans la région du Donbass, dans l'est de l’Ukraine, dont la Russie veut prendre le contrôle intégral. Ces dernières semaines, l'administration du président américain Donald Trump s'est efforcée de relancer les négociations visant à mettre fin à ce conflit - déclenchée par l'invasion à grande échelle de l'Ukraine par la Russie en février 2022 - le plus sanglant que l'Europe ait connu depuis la Deuxième Guerre mondiale. Fin septembre, Volodimir Zelensky s'est entretenu avec Donald Trump en marge de l'Assemblée générale des Nations unies à New York, où ils ont discuté des moyens de mettre fin à la guerre entre l'Ukraine et la Russie. Le 13 septembre, Donald Trump a appelé Volodimir Zelensky à cesser de prendre pour cible [USN:L6N455055 TEXT:"les raffineries russes"] produisant du diesel, liant implicitement la flambée des prix de ce carburant aux États-Unis à la guerre en Ukraine plutôt qu'au conflit au Moyen-Orient qu'il a déclenché. D'après le président ukrainien, rien d'indique Vladimir Poutine est intéressé par des pourparlers de paix ou par un cessez-le-feu concernant les infrastructures énergétiques. Depuis quelques mois, la Russie a imposé à plusieurs reprises des restrictions sur les exportations d'essence, de kérosène et de [USN:L6N45M0ND TEXT:"gazole"] afin de freiner la hausse des prix des carburants et de remédier aux pénuries provoquées par les attaques de drones ukrainiens contre des raffineries. Mercredi, la Russie a une nouvelle fois pris pour cible le [USN:L8N45M03S TEXT:"réseau énergétique ukrainien"], visant notamment la capitale Kyiv et sa région, faisant sept morts, dont un enfant. Et vendredi, une attaque aérienne russe a fait un mort à Kyiv et a conduit à la fermeture dans la matinée de [USN:L8N45O07U TEXT:"deux ponts"] sur le Dniepr, fleuve traversant la capitale ukrainienne. "Nous devons riposter par tous les moyens (à notre disposition). Face à leurs attaques contre notre secteur énergétique, nous devons riposter en ciblant leur secteur énergétique. En premier lieu, les raffineries de pétrole : ce sont elles qui leur fournissent les fonds nécessaires à cette guerre", a déclaré Volodimir Zelensky, s'exprimant en anglais. "Mais nous ne riposterons pas, bien sûr, à l'instar de ce qu'ils font, en visant des cibles civiles", a-t-il ajouté. PAS DE NORMALISATION AVANT UNE PERSPECTIVE DE PAIX Le président ukrainien a exhorté Washington à ne pas normaliser ses relations avec la Russie avant de s'être assuré d'un retour à la paix, réagissant ainsi à l'invitation adressée par Donald Trump à Vladimir Poutine de participer à un sommet du G20 prévu en décembre à Miami. La décision de Washington [USN:L8N44S23E TEXT:"d'autoriser"] Moscou à prendre part début septembre une réunion des pays du G20 tout en interdisant à des journalistes d'y accéder avait déjà irrité certains ministres des Finances de cette instance. Volodomir Zelensky a déclaré qu'il était prêt à rencontrer Vladimir Poutine pour des pourparlers de paix lors du G20, mais il a souligné qu'il ne fallait pas se contenter d'une "normalisation" des rapports avec la Russie. Les responsables ukrainiens notent que la Russie a stocké des centaines de missiles balistiques en prévision d'une offensive hivernale attendue contre les infrastructures électriques et hydrauliques. L'hiver dernier, qui a été le plus dur de la guerre, les frappes russes ont privé de vastes régions du pays d'électricité et de chauffage pendant plusieurs jours d'affilée. Depuis l'été, Moscou a également commencé à lancer chaque jour des dizaines de drones Shahed à réaction, rapides et relativement bon marché, en direction de l'Ukraine, mettant à rude épreuve les défenses anti-aériennes de l'Ukraine. Volodomir Zelensky a précisé que l'Ukraine a eu massivement recours à ses avions de chasse - des F-16 et des MiG - pour abattre environ 60% des drones russes à réaction, tout en ajoutant que les stocks de munitions de 20 mm équipant ces chasseurs s'épuisent. Kyiv travaille d'arrache-pied à la mise au point d'autres solutions - notamment le renforcement de ses capacités de brouillage, a-t-il précisé. La semaine dernière, Volodmir Zelensky a déclaré que l'Ukraine développait cinq modèles de nouveaux drones intercepteurs capables d'abattre les Shahed à réaction. "Nous devrons passer à l'échelle supérieure. J'espère qu'avec tous ces éléments, nous trouverons une solution", a-t-il dit. L'Ukraine a annoncé cette semaine la première utilisation au combat de son propre missile balistique de fabrication nationale, le FP-7, qui dispose d'une portée d’environ 250 kilomètres. Volodomir Zelensky a dit avoir appelé le fabricant de ce missile, Fire Point, pour exhorter ses dirigeants à achever rapidement un modèle à plus longue portée, le FP-9, qui, selon l'entreprise, pourrait atteindre Moscou. "Je leur ai dit : 'Où est mon FP-9 ?'. Nous avons besoin du FP-9. Et le FP-9 sera (prêt) cet automne, j'en suis sûr", a-t-il dit.

item.title: Trump shares Republican senator's phone number in feud over time switch
item.description: US President Donald Trump shared online the supposed phone number of a Republican US senator on Saturday in an escalating dispute over making daylight saving time permanent.
item.dc:creator: Bo Erickson
item.content:encoded: US President Donald Trump shared online the supposed phone number of a Republican US senator on Saturday in an escalating dispute over making daylight saving time permanent. In a social media post, the president urged people to call a phone number he said belonged to Senator Tom Cotton, an Arkansas Republican who opposes the Trump-backed Sunshine Protection Act. The act would end the twice-yearly practice of changing clocks by one hour. Trump says most Americans want more afternoon sunlight, but Cotton has argued the change would plunge early risers into darkness in winter. "Everybody in Arkansas, Tom Cotton, a friend of mine, is holding up a very important Bill," Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform. Cotton did not directly respond to Trump's statement, but posted on X: "No one likes changing the clock, me included, but Congress has enacted permanent Daylight Savings Time multiple times before and repealed it each time once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter. "Arkansans don't want their kids going to school in the pitch dark, and I'll always put Arkansas first." When Reuters called the number Trump gave for Cotton, it went directly to a voicemail box that did not identify itself as belonging to the senator. Supporters of permanent daylight saving time say adjusting clocks disrupts sleep and increases road accidents, while critics argue later winter sunrises would leave children traveling to school and commuters heading to work in the dark. GOLFING ARGUMENT Trump on Saturday published three Truth Social posts — one in the morning and two in the afternoon — focused on daylight saving time. In a subsequent five-minute session with journalists at the White House, he spent more than half the time talking about the twice-yearly practice of changing clocks by one hour . Most US states have observed the time switch since the 1960s. Clocks this year are slated to switch back to standard time on November 1. "It discombobulates everybody," Trump said, complaining to reporters that losing afternoon daylight caused lateness for meetings and dinner and made it difficult to play more than 14 holes of golf. He also suggested that more daylight would reduce crime. "You know who wants it? The farmers want it. You know who wants it? Sports want it," Trump told reporters before heading to a [USN:L1N45O0PX TEXT:"campaign rally in Ohio"] . "Professional sports and amateurs that would like to play tennis at night, would like to play golf a little bit without having to run home after 14 holes." Trump, an avid golfer, earlier shared an October 1 letter from PGA Tour CEO Brian Rolapp, writing: "The PGA TOUR, as an example, needs more Daylight in the afternoon in order to finish their Tournaments." POLITICAL CONSIDERATIONS After Cotton published his statement, the president responded with a post that framed the matter in political terms. "Give the Republican Party a Senatorial WIN, for a change! … TAKE THE WIN TOM, JUST TAKE THE WIN! YOU NEED IT, AND SO DOES OUR BELOVED REPUBLICAN PARTY!" Trump wrote. Cotton is running for reelection but his race is not considered competitive, as Trump received more than 64% of the Arkansas vote in the 2024 presidential election. The US House of Representatives passed the bill in July, but Cotton is not alone in the Senate. Senator John Kennedy, a Louisiana Republican, this week called the bill "[USN:L1N45O0H3 TEXT:"dead as disco"]" and said he did not think that Senate Majority Leader John Thune would bring the measure for a vote. The offices of Cotton and Thune did not respond to requests for comment. Saturday's post targeting Cotton is not the first time Trump has shared a senator's phone number to make a point. During his first presidential campaign in 2015, Trump [USN:KCN0PV26U TEXT:"read"] Senator Lindsey Graham's phone number at a rally and dismissed the South Carolina Republican as an "idiot." They later reconciled, with the [USN:L6N43E02O TEXT:"late Graham"] becoming one of Trump's highest-profile allies in Congress.

item.title: Padres' Walker Buehler begins NLDS on paternity leave
item.description: Major League Baseball announced Saturday that San Diego Padres right-hander Walker Buehler has been placed on the postseason paternity list.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Major League Baseball announced Saturday that San Diego Padres right-hander Walker Buehler has been placed on the postseason paternity list. During the two-time All-Star's absence, right-hander Randy Vasquez will be on the active roster for the National League Division Series against the Brewers, which begins Saturday night in Milwaukee. Buehler, 32, is permitted to be away from the Padres for one to three days. Upon his return, he will replace Vazquez on the NLDS roster. "Exciting time for him and his wife to be having a baby this weekend, happens to be during the Division Series, which is exciting," San Diego manager Craig Stammen said prior to Game 1. "Don't have any word on what's going on yet but it could happen at any moment. I'm sure there will be stuff that comes out when it does happen. But excited for the Buehler family." Game 1 of the best-of-five series would have been Buehler's turn in the rotation. He held the Brewers to one run on three hits in six innings in an 11-2 victory in San Diego on Aug. 11. Game 2 is Sunday in Milwaukee. The earliest Buehler can pitch is Game 3 when the series shifts to San Diego on Tuesday night. Left-hander Robbie Ray is the Padres' scheduled starter for Game 1, followed by right-hander Michael King for Game 2. Ray will be opposed by hard-throwing right-hander Jacob Misiorowski (16-5, 1.80 ERA), who leads the majors in ERA and strikeouts (252 in 174 2/3 innings). Buehler's wife, McKenzie, is expected to give birth to their second child on Saturday, according to the San Diego Union-Tribune. Their daughter, Finley, was born in January 2024. Buehler stayed behind in San Diego when the club traveled to Milwaukee. "I think we didn't want Walker having to pitch on a possible day of the birth of his child and miss that," Stammen said. "I think it made sense that he's able to stay in San Diego and allow that to happen and not having to worry about pitching and that going on at the same time." Buehler was 9-6 with a 4.63 ERA in 32 starts in his first season with the Padres. A two-time World Series champion with the Los Angeles Dodgers, Buehler did not pitch in the NL wild-card sweep against the Chicago Cubs. He is 4-4 with a 3.04 ERA in 19 appearances (18 starts) in the postseason. Vasquez, 27, was 10-6 with a 3.90 ERA in 32 games (23 starts) this season for San Diego. --Field Level Media

item.title: Ukraine will hit Russian refineries in response to Moscow's 'new doctrine' of airstrikes, Zelenskiy says
item.description: Ukrainian intelligence has documents showing that Vladimir Putin called for military attacks on a much broader range of civilian targets ahead of this winter, Zelenskiy told Reuters in an interview.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Flynn, Olena Harmash
item.content:encoded: Ukraine will double down on attacking Russian oil refineries in response to a new policy of airstrikes by Moscow designed to [USN:L8N44V1KC TEXT:"force people to abandon Kyiv"] and other cities, but will not target civilians, President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said. Ukraine's intelligence services has obtained documents showing that Russian leader Vladimir Putin had issued a "new doctrine" of military attacks on a much broader range of civilian targets ahead of this winter, Zelenskiy said. "We saw documents and we know that they allow them to attack infrastructure, logistics, and especially to attack in the cities, in the villages, everywhere, roads, schools, hospitals," Zelenskiy told Reuters in an interview. "To pressure people to leave the capital, leave different cities: this is the goal of the operation." Driving the shift in policy, Zelenskiy said, was Putin's desire to appear strong at a time when his military was losing ground in a key frontline region and sustaining higher levels of casualties. The Kremlin was not available to comment on Saturday. But in a statement [USN:L1N45P03K TEXT:"urging foreign nationals to leave Kyiv"], the Russian Foreign Ministry said Moscow would continue to systematically hit targets in what it said were retaliatory strikes for Ukrainian attacks on Russia in recent months. Both sides deny deliberately targeting civilians. COUNTEROFFENSIVE IN DONBAS Zelenskiy said a successful Ukrainian counteroffensive, code-named "Vivaldi", had recaptured around 140 sq km (54 sq miles) of Ukrain's eastern Donbas region and was still ongoing. Russia has said it must control Donbas in its entirety as a condition for any peace deal. In recent weeks, US President Donald Trump's administration has sought to revive talks to end the four-year-old conflict – Europe's bloodiest since World War Two. The US leader last month urged Ukraine [USN:L1N45503J TEXT:"to refrain from hitting Russian oil installations"], saying that was sending global diesel prices surging. But Zelenskiy, speaking as air raid sirens blared outside the gilded halls of the presidential offices, said he had received no indications from Russia that Putin was interested in peace talks, or discussing a ceasefire on energy infrastructure. Over the past week, the Ukrainian capital has come under persistent attack by Russian drones and missiles targeting energy and telecoms assets, road and rail infrastructure. For the first time, Russia has [USN:L1N45P00Z TEXT:"targeted the bridges"] across the Dnipro river connecting east and west Kyiv. Zelenskiy said Ukraine would react to the change in tactics by Moscow, but would not target civilian infrastructure indiscriminately. "We have to respond in any way (we can). With their attacks on our energy, we have to respond on their energy. First of all, oil refiners etc: what gives money to them for this war," Zelenskiy said in English. "But we will not respond, of course, just like them, on any civilian objects." SUPPORT FROM EUROPE After the Trump administration invited Putin [USN:L6N45F16H TEXT:"to attend a G20 summit in Miami"] in December and discussed business deals with Russian envoys, Zelenskiy urged Washington not to normalise relations with Russia before ensuring a return to peace. Zelenskiy said he would be happy to meet Putin for peace talks at the G20, but he warned the US not to believe in "illusions" that Russia would simply end hostilities if it gained control of Donbas. "It's not fair just to normalise," said Zelenskiy, dressed in his trademark black T-shirt and military-style jacket. Any resumption of economic and diplomatic ties with the West had to be in return for Russia ending hostilities, he said: "Because peace is more important than any kind of economy." While the US has proposed a resumption of trilateral talks in the coming weeks in the UAE, Zelenskiy noted that an exact date and location for the technical-level conversations had still not been set. Ukrainian officials warn that Russia has stockpiled hundreds of ballistic missiles ahead of an expected winter onslaught against electricity and water infrastructure. Last winter, the worst of the war, Russian strikes left swathes of the country without electricity and heating for days at a time. Since the summer, Moscow has also begun launching dozens of fast and relatively cheap jet-powered Shahed drones a day at Ukraine, whose air defence teams have struggled to cope because their interceptor drones were too slow to catch them. Zelenskiy said Ukraine had been forced to rely heavily on its fighter aircraft – F-16s and MiGs – to down around 60% of the Russian jet-powered drones, but supplies of 20 mm ammunition for the planes were running low. Kyiv was urgently working on other solutions – including boosting its electronic jamming capabilities, he said. In the second half of October, it would receive the first shipment of small, cheap air defence missiles capable of hitting the new Shaheds. Last week, Zelenskiy said Ukraine was developing five models of new interceptor drones capable of downing the jet Shaheds. Fresh from a meeting with his defence chiefs, he said tests on two of those models showed a modest success rate of around 30%. "We'll have to scale it," he said. "I hope that with all these things, with all these elements, we'll find a way." BALLISTIC THREAT Ukraine announced the first combat use this week of its own domestically made ballistic missile, the FP-7, which has a range of around 250 km (155 miles). Zelenskiy said he had called the manufacturer Fire Point to pressure executives to finish a longer-range model, the FP-9, which the company has said could hit Moscow. "I said to them, where is my FP-9?" said Zelenskiy, with a grin. "We need the FP-9. And the FP-9 will be (ready) this autumn, I'm sure." Zelenskiy said a recent spate of Russian drone incursions and hybrid attacks in Europe were an effort to intimidate European populations and to undermine support for Ukraine. Some European leaders were starting to understand this, he said, and toughen their position. Russia says such accusations are baseless and the result of anti-Russian hysteria. After talks with European officials in Brussels this week, Ukraine had unlocked funding to order the drones that it needs to keep fighting at the start of 2027, Zelenskiy said. Ukrainian officials had worked on plans with European partners to plug a $27 billion hole in Kyiv's defence budget this year. The plans involve a combination of the reallocation of Ukraine's own budget resources, bilateral assistance and using "money credits" from next year's portion of a €90 billion EU loan, Zelenskiy said. "We will close this (gap). I think this is absolutely a big success for our country," he said.

item.title: OF Aaron Judge (calf) left off Yankees' ALDS roster
item.description: Captain Aaron Judge was left off the New York Yankees' roster for their American League Division Series against the Tampa Bay Rays.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Captain Aaron Judge was left off the New York Yankees' roster for their American League Division Series against the Tampa Bay Rays. The Yankees revealed their 26-man roster for the best-of-five series on Saturday morning, with Game 1 set for 6:38 p.m. ET in St. Petersburg, Fla. Judge, 34, has not played since Sept. 16 with a strained right calf. The three-time AL MVP landed on the injured list three days later and missed the Yankees' two-game wild-card sweep against the rival Boston Red Sox earlier this week. "Ultimately, I obviously decided keeping (Judge off the roster) was the best thing," Yankees manager Aaron Boone said. "Again, I feel like he's getting close, but I feel like for us to get a version of Aaron back and to win a World Series, I feel like this week's important for him to continue to work towards getting back. He just started running. He's hit now a couple of days. So I think another several days of doing that and building some endurance, I think, is important. "Understanding entirely that we're guaranteed nothing. (If) we don't play well, next week we're home and we don't get it. But I feel like for us to get a good version of Aaron, this was the right thing to do." Judge faced live pitching for the first time since the injury on Monday, was running in the outfield on Tuesday and took batting practice on Wednesday and Thursday. The outfielder participated in workouts on Friday at the Yankees' minor league facility in Tampa and also at Tropicana Field. Judge has voiced his determination to return in the postseason, but the team ultimately decided to move forward without him against Tampa Bay. Trent Grisham, Spencer Jones, Heliot Ramos and Giancarlo Stanton are the outfielders on the ALDS roster set to face the Rays. Boone said Stanton is only available for pinch-hitting. Stanton hasn't played in a game since April 24. "If there's any time to erase a bad year, it's in October," Stanton said. "It's the biggest opportunity to show out for the city and do what we can do." Cody Bellinger and Jose Caballero, who can play in both the infield and outfield, are listed as utility players. Judge largely was ineffective before the calf injury, batting .174 (4-for-23) with a homer and three RBIs in seven games after his Sept. 8 return from the injured list. He had missed more than three months with a fractured rib. "Yeah, but it's more about the endurance, more about the going out there and playing a baseball game for three hours," Boone said. "I mean, he hasn't done anything really for a couple weeks in that regard. That's the challenge of all this." In 66 games overall this year, Judge batted .241 with a .360 on-base percentage, a .511 slugging percentage, 18 homers and 41 RBIs. That is the fewest number of games Judge has played since his 2016 debut season, not including the 2020 pandemic campaign. An eight-time All-Star, Judge still is looking for his first World Series championship. He is a career .236 hitter in the postseason with 17 home runs and 41 RBIs in 65 games. --Field Level Media

item.title: Lula ahead in polls for Brazil's first-round vote; runoff likely
item.description: A series of polls on Saturday showed Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva slightly ahead of Senator Flavio Bolsonaro before Sunday's first-round vote, and a close race in a likely runoff between the leftist incumbent and his right-wing challenger.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: A series of polls on Saturday showed Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva slightly ahead of Senator Flavio Bolsonaro before Sunday's first-round vote, and a close race in a likely runoff between the leftist incumbent and his right-wing challenger. If no candidate wins more than 50% of valid votes -- which exclude blank and null ballots -- on Sunday, the two frontrunners advance to a second-round runoff on October 25. item.title: US Coast Guard finds debris from missing medical aircraft off Nantucket
item.description: The US Coast Guard said late on Saturday it found debris from a medical transport aircraft off the shore of Massachusetts' Nantucket island and was searching for six people who were on board.
item.dc:creator: Sheila Dang, Lisa Richwine
item.content:encoded: The US Coast Guard said late on Saturday it found debris from a medical transport aircraft off the shore of Massachusetts' Nantucket island and was searching for six people who were on board. The Federal Aviation Administration told the Coast Guard early on Saturday that it had lost contact with a Gulfstream jet traveling from Bermuda to Boston. Several hours later, the Coast Guard said in a statement that it "located a debris field that has been confirmed to be associated with the missing aircraft." Four Canadians were on the plane, Canadian Minister of Transport Steven MacKinnon said on X. "We are closely monitoring the situation and are working with the relevant authorities as search and rescue efforts continue," he wrote. The other two passengers were Bermudian nationals, the Coast Guard said. Searches will continue throughout the night near Nantucket, an island community south of mainland Massachusetts, they said. The aircraft, registered to Latitude Air Ambulance, departed Bermuda at 12:41 a.m. on Saturday (0301 GMT), according to data from flight tracking website FlightAware. The plane was flying at 24,000 feet (7,300 metres) for much of the flight before descending 13,000 feet in about two minutes shortly before flight controllers lost contact, data showed. Local TV station Boston 25 posted an audio clip from Boston Logan International Airport in which an air traffic controller can be heard asking the Gulfstream pilot, "You said you're coming in blind? Is that what you said?" The controller then asked whether the plane was declaring an emergency. No response was heard. Latitude is based in Ontario, Canada, and provides medical evacuation services. The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The Bermuda government is in contact with US authorities and the families of the passengers, Bermuda Premier David Burt wrote in a statement posted on Instagram. "We are praying that all six people will be found safe," he wrote.

item.title: Portugal prosecutors probe legality of US use of Lajes base in Iran war
item.description: A longstanding agreement with the US allows it to use the Azores air base without prior authorization during peacetime.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Portuguese prosecutors said on Saturday they had opened a probe into the legality of the centre-right government's authorisation of the United States' use of the Lajes Air Base in the Azores during the Iran conflict, following a complaint by an opposition party. A longstanding agreement with the US allows Washington to use the base without prior authorisation during peacetime, but requires Portugal to give approval once hostilities begin. Portugal, unlike neighbouring Spain, [USN:L8N3ZS22H TEXT:"authorised several US transit flights"] through the Lajes air base, a decision that drew criticism from left-wing opposition parties and triggered a political debate over Lisbon's role in operations linked to the conflict with Iran. In a statement, the Prosecutor General's Office said "the probe was opened following a complaint filed by members of the Left Bloc party," without providing further details. Portugal's Foreign Ministry declined to comment. The Left Bloc asked prosecutors in April to investigate the US use of the Lajes base, arguing it amounted to a "gross violation of international law." However, Foreign Minister Paulo Rangel has said Portugal was not involved in the conflict and that the use of the Lajes base complied with international law, having been authorised only after assurances from Washington that any operation would be defensive, necessary and proportionate, and limited to military targets. Portugal's prosecutors are bound by the principle of legality, requiring them to investigate alleged wrongdoing when there are sufficient grounds to do so, unlike in some jurisdictions where prosecutors have broader discretion to decide whether a case should proceed. The Lajes base, located in Portugal's Atlantic Azores archipelago, is a strategic transit hub for US forces under a bilateral defence treaty dating back to 1951 and hosts the 65th Air Base Wing of the US Air Force, providing support for US, NATO and allied operations.

item.title: Tens of thousands protest across Spain over housing crisis
item.description: Anger swelled over the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her apartment in Madrid.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Spanish police arrested three members of a far-right group and fired rubber bullets on Saturday night in Madrid after tens of thousands had marched across the country to demand action to tackle a housing crisis. Far-right activists, some of whom performed Nazi salutes, tried to reach demonstrators camped out in the Puerta del Sol, a central square in the Spanish capital, to protest the housing crisis, the Spanish government said. Earlier, some demonstrators waved posters calling for a general strike after the measures drawn up to address mass anger over the eviction of an 87-year-old woman in Madrid, and other housing issues, were [USN:L8N45F0PQ TEXT:"rejected"] in parliament on Friday. "It's a shame," said Nando de Anguulo, 26, who joined Saturday's protest in Madrid. "It only proves that it is us, the people, who have to adapt to the political parties, and not the politicians to what the people want, and this can't go on like that." Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez might call a snap election for November after the legislation failed to pass and would be watching the strength of Saturday's protests before deciding, Spanish media reported on Friday. Sanchez's office declined to comment on the reports. In the southeastern city of Valencia, demonstrators clashed with police who fired rubber bullets and tear gas to break up protests. About 30 protesters entered the City of Arts and Sciences, a landmark cultural complex, before police ousted them. Other demonstrations in 50 Spanish cities were peaceful. Valeria Racu, spokesperson for the Tenants Union, told reporters in Madrid that a general strike would be called after talks with labour unions. About 70,000 protesters took part in Saturday's demonstration in Madrid, the Spanish government said. Protests planned in Barcelona and the nearby city of Hospitalet de Llobregat were called off because of heavy rain.

LONDON: Two Iranian nationals appeared in a London court on Saturday (Oct 3) charged with plotting acts of terrorism involving the use of a homemade bomb to attack the Jewish community in northern England at the behest of a figure believed to be based in Iran. Rahman Salehi, 34, and Salam Ahmadyan, 36, were arrested on Sep 20 at the start of Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar, when they are accused of carrying out "hostile" surveillance on potential Jewish targets in Manchester, prosecutors say. These targets included the Manchester Jewish Museum and Heaton Park synagogue, the scene of a deadly attack almost a year ago in which two Jewish worshippers were killed, prosecutor Mark Luckett told Westminster Magistrates' Court. ALLEGED PLOT INVOLVED HOMEMADE DEVICE "Both defendants are accused of preparing acts of terrorism targeting the Jewish community in Manchester through the use of a homemade explosive device," Luckett said.

He said the men were accused of being in contact with a third party who is alleged to have directed and coordinated the attack planning and provided instructions on how to assemble a homemade device, which prosecutors allege would have been made from chlorine and brake fluid. "It's assessed that this individual is also an Iranian national and most likely operating from within Iran," Luckett said.

Related:

UK's Starmer convenes community leaders to fight antisemitism after attacks

Two Jewish men stabbed in London, police treat attack as terrorism

The court was told both men had come to Britain from Europe in small boats. Salehi had arrived in 2020 and had been granted asylum, while Ahmadyan came in 2023 and his asylum claim was still outstanding, Luckett said. The men did not enter a plea and were remanded in custody until their next hearing at London's Old Bailey court on Oct 23. The case comes a week after Britain said Iran was believed to be involved in a suspected plot to target the RAF Fairford air base which the US military has used to carry out raids against targets in Iran, leading to a dual British-Iranian national being arrested on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts. Police said on Saturday he had been released on police bail while the investigation continues. British counterterrorism police have said the Manchester allegations were not connected in any way to the Fairford investigation. Iran has rejected accusations of involvement in a number of plots in Britain in recent years, and said allegations it was connected to the Fairford incident were baseless. Britain has also seen a significant rise in antisemitism since the Hamas attacks on Israel in October 2023 that triggered the subsequent war in Gaza, including a series of attacks on Jewish sites in London earlier this year. "It is no secret that this country faces a range of serious threats from the Iranian regime," Home Secretary (interior minister) Shabana Mahmood said in a statement. "They target our Jewish communities and try to silence their critics overseas, often through proxies and criminal networks to hide their involvement."

Source: Reuters/ec

item.title: Les Houthis revendiquent l'attaque d'un site Aramco à Ryad
item.description: Les rebelles houthis du Yémen ont annoncé avoir attaqué samedi un site d'Aramco, la compagnie pétrolière nationale de l'Arabie saoudite, situé à Ryad, capitale du royaume, avec des missiles balistiques et des drones.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Les rebelles houthis du Yémen ont annoncé avoir attaqué samedi un site d'Aramco, la compagnie pétrolière nationale de l'Arabie saoudite, situé à Ryad, capitale du royaume, avec des missiles balistiques et des drones. L'Arabie saoudite n'a pas confirmé à ce stade cette information. Plus tôt dans la journée, un journaliste de Reuters a fait état d'un important panache de fumée et de flammes s'élevant à proximité d'un site de Saudi Aramco à Ryad. Aramco n'a pas répondu pour le moment à une demande de commentaires. L'incendie survient dans un contexte d'escalade des hostilités entre l'Arabie saoudite et les Houthis yéménites, proches de l'Iran, qui ont intensifié leurs attaques contre les villes et les infrastructures énergétiques saoudiennes. Les Houthis ont déclaré la semaine dernière avoir attaqué des installations d'Aramco à Yanbu à l'aide de missiles et de drones. L'Arabie saoudite avait alors dit avoir intercepté six missiles balistiques tirés par les Houthis en direction de Taïf et de la région de Yanbu, mais n'avait pas fait état de dégâts sur les installations d'Aramco.

item.title: Yemen's Houthis say they attacked Aramco facility in Riyadh with missiles, drones
item.description: There was no immediate confirmation from Saudi authorities of an attack on an Aramco facility.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said on Saturday they had targeted an Aramco facility in the Saudi capital Riyadh with ballistic missiles and drones, saying the attack was in retaliation for Saudi attacks on Yemen's Sanaa and other provinces. A large plume of smoke and fire was seen rising in the vicinity of an Aramco facility in Riyadh earlier on Saturday, a witness told Reuters. There was no immediate confirmation from Saudi authorities of an attack on an Aramco facility. Aramco did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The reported attack comes amid escalating hostilities between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, who have stepped up attacks on Saudi cities and energy infrastructure. The Houthis said last week they had attacked Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu with missiles and drones. Saudi Arabia said at the time that it had intercepted six ballistic missiles fired by the Houthis towards Taif and the Yanbu area, but did not report damage to Aramco facilities.

item.title: Ireland coach Hallgrimsson hopes squad bonds will be stronger after tough period
item.description: Ireland coach Heimir Hallgrimsson has said his side will come out of the international window stronger after two fractious games against Israel that fans and politicians had called on his side to boycott.
item.dc:creator: Fatos Bytyci
item.content:encoded: Ireland coach Heimir Hallgrimsson has said his side will come out of the international window stronger after two fractious games against Israel that fans and politicians had [USN:L6N45I06Z TEXT:"called on his side to boycott"]. The matches had been a focus of attention since the sides were drawn together in February, with Ireland one of Europe's most outspoken critics of Israel's war in Gaza . There have been numerous protests in Ireland asking for the team not to fulfil the fixtures with Israel. Such was the opposition to the Irish team playing Israel that the Football Association of Ireland chose to hold the game behind closed doors in Backa Topola, a small Serbian town of around 12,000 people, rather than in Dublin. Reserve goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu, who declined to be in the squad for the first game against Israel, will again be missing when the two sides meet in Serbia on Sunday, and captain Dara O’Shea will also miss out due to the birth of his child. “Football-wise, what's to come most of all is to control our focus level and keep the focus on that one (Sunday’s game against Israel), don't lose it,” the Icelandic coach told a press conference on Saturday. “There's been a lot of emotions from the people in Ireland about this, and obviously that affects the players as well. We want to do good, but it's always going to be a challenge when the environment is as noisy as it is.” TWO PROTESTS Thursday’s 2-2 draw with Austria in Dublin was briefly disrupted by two protests, but a superb goal from Troy Parrott against the Austrians and four points from their last two games have eased the pressure on the Irish team. The FAI is continuing to investigate allegations that Irish players Adam Idah and James Abankwah were racially abused in Sunday’s 3-0 win over the Israelis in Hungary. “It just goes to a process both in our departments and then to UEFA to look at,” Hallgrimsson said. “It was something that was reported from both teams. I just hope that we can focus on football and that football will be the winner after this.” The 59-year-old said the difficulties the team had faced would strengthen them. “Surviving this camp, coming out of it together as one, would be a massive win for me, that is coming from my heart,” he said. “I think all the challenges that this team has gone through, all the criticism, yeah, I think just surviving as a group after this game, that will be a big win for me and for this group, (and) for the (football) association.” The news conference ended abruptly when an Israeli journalist asked about an allegation that an Irish player had called an Israeli player "a monkey" during Sunday's game, with Irish press officer Kieran Crowley strongly denying the allegation before quickly bringing it to a close. Israel coach Ran Ben-Shimon refused to be drawn into off-field matters. "This game is very important to us, (the) point(s) matter to come back to the group, and I'm focusing on how can I lead my team to have a good result tomorrow. This is my only focus, you can trust me on this," he told reporters. Austria top Group B3 on seven points, with Kosovo second on four ahead of the Irish on goal difference, and Israel bottom with one point.

item.title: In crude Ohio rally speech, Trump says he may not help if Democrats win
item.description: Sen. Jon Husted is hoping Trump can motivate supporters who might otherwise skip voting.
item.dc:creator: Bo Erickson, Nandita Bose
item.content:encoded: US President Donald Trump used an Ohio rally on Saturday to mix profane attacks on Democrats with promises of financial help if Republicans win the midterms and a warning that he would be less willing to work with the state if Democrats prevail. "Just get out and vote," Trump said at a rally for Republican candidates, including US Senator Jon Husted and Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy. "If you do that, we're going to win, and we're going to win big, and we're going to shove it up their ass." Multiple incumbent Republican senators across the country face tough political headwinds in the November 3 elections, with Trump's [USN:L6N45D0XN TEXT:"popularity falling"] in recent months as higher prices persist for gasoline and other staples amid the US-Israeli war with Iran. Both Husted and Ramaswamy are in competitive races against Democratic opponents. Former US Senator Sherrod Brown is running against Husted. Amy Acton is facing Ramaswamy. OHIO A KEY STATE IN MIDTERMS Polls have suggested that Democrats could gain ground in the midterms, which will decide control of the narrowly divided House of Representatives and Senate, but Trump said Republicans would do better than critics expect. "I think we're going to have a big surprise because they don't know what's happening," he told the crowd in Vandalia, Ohio. Ohio's is among eight US Senate races rated competitive. The state has turned into a campaign battlefield over [USN:L6N45916H TEXT:"data centers"] and culture war issues such as youth transgender surgeries. Trump repeatedly attacked Democrats during his speech, at one point calling them "dumb son of a bitches," while arguing that maintaining Republican control would give Ohio officials a direct line to his administration and make it easier for the state to secure federal help. He said Ohio's elected Republican officials frequently call him seeking money for the state, adding that he would be less inclined to accommodate Democrats if they win key races. Referring to Acton, Trump said: "But I'm not going to help her." Husted is counting on Trump to motivate supporters who might otherwise skip the midterms, but the senator also directly criticized Brown, a veteran Democrat, as someone who has accomplished little in his political career. "He's been in office for 50 years — can you name one thing that he has done for you?" Husted said at the rally. A spokesperson for Brown's campaign criticized Husted for backing Trump's policy on Iran and said Husted supported "sweetheart tax deals" that lured data centers to Ohio. "Jon Husted puts corporations and billionaires first every time, and we all pay for it," Brown spokesperson Lauren Chou said in an email to Reuters. Trump garnered more than 55% of the Ohio vote in the 2024 presidential election, but economic concerns since then have sunk his approval ratings. Ohio gasoline prices increased 35% over the past year to $4.16 per gallon on average, according to AAA, which compiles data on automobile travel. Trump's trade policy with Canada has led to retaliatory Canadian tariffs that affect about $3 billion worth of Ohio exports, based on 2025 figures, according to a CBC report. DEBATE ON DATA CENTERS Talking to reporters shortly before addressing Saturday's rally, Husted said the US has to win the Iran war "on our terms" and in the interim, he is "showing people that I'm fighting for lower prices." He spoke to a sympathetic crowd at the rally, but he also needs to sell his message to people like independent voter Jonathan Smith. Smith, a 19-year-old construction worker, held a sign reading, "Where are my lower gas prices?" outside his former high school in Vandalia, north of Dayton. "I've got a wedding to save up for, and with gas prices continuously going up, it's getting harder and harder to put aside money," said Smith, adding he is still deciding whom to vote for in the Senate race. Outside political groups have poured [USN:L6N458188 TEXT:"tens of millions"] of dollars into Ohio, making Husted-Brown the second-most-expensive Senate race in the country, according to Federal Election Commission filings. Rallygoers shared mixed opinions on the hot-button issue of data centers in the state. "I'm not huge on the AI data centers," Samuel Clevenger, 20, said when discussing Husted's candidacy. But the apprentice plumber said he was encouraged to vote by Trump's attention to the state, as well as his 2025 policy capping taxes on overtime. On the other side of the rally venue, Brenda White, 60, held a sign encouraging building in her northeastern Ohio town: "DATA CENTER SOUTH LORAIN." As Husted met voters in the bleachers, she urged the senator to support the center's construction in place of a steel mill. "You want a data center there?" Husted asked. Before White posed for her photo with Husted, a man in the senator's entourage asked: "Can we do it without the sign?"

FAST

WASHINGTON, Oct 3 : US President Donald Trump spent Tuesday showcasing his administration’s approach to AI — touting the US government’s new AI chatbot, dining with tech titans at the White House, and announcing a voluntary agreement with those executives that he said would address growing fears about the technology's safety. The display signaled that Trump is eager to show he is addressing growing voter concerns about AI's dangers without imposing restrictions that could hamper the technology's development, AI safety advocates said. The safety agreement with six companies — Nvidia, SpaceX, OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and Alphabet’s Google — includes no stated consequences if a company chooses not to comply. Trump described it as “morally binding.” “This was an attempt to give the impression that the government is listening to these concerns without undercutting what has been a very clear and consistent line from this administration: that regulation and governance inherently impede innovation,” said Kat Duffy, who runs an AI team at the nonpartisan Council on Foreign Relations. Whether voters buy Trump's effort in the run-up to US midterm elections on November 3 remains to be seen. Public uneasiness with AI, and the small group of people who seemingly hold sway over it, has risen in recent months. Three-quarters of Americans worry that AI companies have not gone far enough to prevent AI from causing serious harm to society, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll published September 22. A series of security events has also underscored how advanced AI can act unpredictably.

Hundreds of OpenAI AI agents broke out of their testing environment in July and attacked the infrastructure of AI platform Hugging Face. In early September, Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned, saying that the people building AI believe it "could kill us all by the end of the decade." His words, and others, sparked a flurry of calls from US lawmakers for AI regulation.  Through it all, Trump has largely dismissed those concerns, saying that government restrictions would make it harder for American companies to compete against their Chinese counterparts. He has repeatedly said that US law enforcement agencies such as the Justice Department serve as sufficient guardrails, and that no new rules are needed. He also directed his administration to call AI "super intelligence," part of an effort to improve the reputation of an unpopular technology.  The concerns have become prominent enough to make their way into late-night comedy. In late September, "Saturday Night Live" satirized Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, one of the industry's most outspoken voices on AI risks — even as his company readies a public stock sale that could value it at $2 trillion — with cast member Jane Wickline portraying the executive. "AI is not a weapon, it’s a tool: A tool for building weapons. And I urge you to urge me to stop," Wickline said as Amodei. CONCERNS ABOUT ENFORCEMENT The accord, inked Tuesday, does include measures that AI safety advocates have sought, including calling for “robust internal controls” to prevent unauthorized hacks as well as partnering with “independent external auditors.” Those concepts have been included in draft state and federal legislation, and California in September enacted the first state law setting rules for how independent auditors evaluate AI products. But the one-page White House document did not address details or enforcement mechanisms. A White House official said in a statement that the agreement will "advance American innovation and strengthen responsible development" of AI models. Trump is expected to name his Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton as his top AI adviser, Reuters previously reported, a position he has dubbed "AI czar," even as Clayton stays in his role leading the nation's intelligence agencies. Representative Ro Khanna, a Democrat representing Silicon Valley, welcomed the idea of "independent auditors" but said that they should report to an independent federal agency. "They can’t just be auditors that report to (OpenAI CEO) Sam Altman or Dario Amodei," he said. "My concern is the president basically trusting these guys who have a huge profit motive and won’t have the judgment to keep us safe." Venture capitalist David Sacks, who advises Trump on AI and has been an advocate for unrestricted AI development, said on the social media platform X that securities law and other legal authorities would penalize companies that fail to address problems uncovered by internal controls or auditors. But AI safety advocates told Reuters those authorities can only address harms after they occur, saying the threats require safeguards designed to prevent large-scale harm before it happens. Nevertheless, some AI observers saw the simple fact of hosting the event as an indication that Trump is absorbing the worries. Trump’s agreement with the tech executives is “a shift toward acknowledging that there are serious safety and security concerns that merit closer coordination between the companies,” said Samuel Hammond, AI policy director at the conservative Foundation for American Innovation.

Source: Reuters

item.title: Russia strikes key Kyiv bridge, logistics hub in latest attacks on Ukraine
item.description: Traffic on Kyiv's Northern Bridge was halted after the strike damaged its surface and trolleybus power lines, while Moscow said it also hit a logistics centre and a cargo vessel ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: Russian forces hit a major bridge in Kyiv that connects the left and right banks of the Dnipro River, as well as a logistics center near the capital overnight, in the latest series of drone attacks on Ukraine’s civil infrastructure. Traffic across Kyiv’s Northern or Pivnichnyi Bridge has been halted, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said in a Telegram statement on Saturday. The strike damaged the bridge’s surface and overhead electrical wires of the city’s trolleybus network, he said. The attack follows a series of strikes on Kyiv’s Southern road-and-rail bridge across the Dnipro earlier this week, which created logistical issues across Ukraine’s capital.  Russia’s Defense Ministry confirmed the latest attack, saying in a statement that the bridge it was being used to transport military cargoes. Russian forces also hit the Hostomel logistics center near Kyiv and a cargo vessel en route to the Black Sea port of Odesa, the ministry said. Russia has intensified its attacks on Ukrainian civil infrastructure in the recent weeks, targeting residential areas, data centers and energy facilities, as well as sea terminals and cargo vessels in a move to disrupt agricultural exports across the Black Sea and make the coming winter more difficult for Ukraine.  Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the Financial Times this week that the increase in strikes on civilian targets comes as Russian President Vladimir Putin instructed his military leaders to abandon the rules of war. Zelenskyy cited intelligence intercepted by Kyiv. Russia hasn’t commented.  Airstrikes are now happening round the clock as Moscow has ramped up production of ballistic missiles and jet-powered Shahed drones, while Kyiv has faced a shortage of Patriot interceptors.  Russia is looking to intensify attacks on Ukraine’s largest cities, including the capital and Odesa on the Black Sea coast, to isolate them as winter sets in, Zelenskyy said. Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine is well into its fifth year.  Separately, the Russian defense ministry said that 218 Ukrainian drones had been downed over Russia between 8 p.m. on Friday and 8 a.m. on Saturday. In Kaluga, less that 100 miles (161 kilometers) south of Moscow, Ukrainian drones damaged several residential buildings, with minor injuries reported, local governor Vladislav Shapsha said in a Telegram statement.

item.description: Monday's (Sep 28) Kyauktaw airstrike, Rakhine's deadliest such attack since a December hospital bombing, killed 50 people and wounded dozens more.

Monday's (Sep 28) Kyauktaw airstrike, Rakhine's deadliest such attack since a December hospital bombing, killed 50 people and wounded dozens more.

Vehicles pass by a person and motorcycles lying on a bridge as fire burns nearby following a Myanmar military airstrike, according to a rebel group that controls the area and a local aid worker, in Kyauktaw, Rakhine State, Myanmar, in this screen grab obtained from a social media video released Sep 28, 2026. MANILA: The Philippines, chair of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), expressed concern over an airstrike in Myanmar's Rakhine state that caused deaths, injuries and destruction, and stood ready to facilitate discussions within the regional bloc on how best to assist Myanmar. "The Philippines is closely monitoring developments and expresses concern over the attacks which resulted in destruction, loss of lives and injuries to those affected," Foreign Affairs Assistant Secretary for ASEAN Affairs Ana Marie Hernando said in an email response on Saturday (Oct 3). As ASEAN chair, Manila said it remained mindful of the views of all member states and would continue to be guided by the regional bloc's consensus-based approach. The Philippines said it stood ready to facilitate discussions within ASEAN on ways to assist Myanmar, in line with the common aspiration of finding a solution that is "Myanmar-owned and led". Monday's Kyauktaw airstrike, Rakhine's deadliest such attack since a December hospital bombing, killed 50 people and wounded dozens more. Myanmar has been locked in a nationwide civil war since a 2021 coup, with an alliance of armed groups, including the Arakan Army, fighting against the military. The protracted conflict has since killed around 100,000 people and displaced more than 3.5 million in the impoverished Southeast Asian nation.

Source: Reuters/js

item.title: High school students in Paris' deprived suburbs spark national protest movement
item.description: While France ranks in the middle of OECD countries for spending on education, the average expenditure per secondary school student has remained little changed over the last decade.
item.dc:creator: CNA
item.content:encoded:
Advertisement

World

High school students in Paris' deprived suburbs spark national protest movement

While France ranks in the middle of OECD countries for spending on education, the average expenditure per secondary school student has remained little changed over the last decade.

Police officers stand in front of protestors amid tear gas as protesting students carry out blockading action near the Kerichen high school in Brest, western France, on Oct 2, 2026. (Photo: AFP/Fred Tanneau)

03 Oct 2026 03:36PM (Updated: 03 Oct 2026 03:42PM)

FAST

AUBERVILLIERS: Maisa, a 17-year-old in a poor Paris suburb who aspires to be an English teacher, joined tens of thousands of other students and their supporters this week in protests that spread across France over dilapidated schools, classroom overcrowding and teacher shortages.  At Lycee Le Corbusier school in Aubervilliers, a suburb north of Paris in the Seine-Saint-Denis department, protesters said schools in poor neighbourhoods like theirs faced the worst conditions. “Last year I took the high school French exam without a French teacher, and teachers have a huge impact,” Maisa said. "These are not conditions to study in."

As protests raged at more than 1,200 French high schools this week, police responded with tear gas and rubber bullets in some cases. More than 5,000 people were arrested, and some protesters were seriously hurt with eye injuries, broken teeth and blows to the head. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez called it a "climate of unacceptable violence" and called for order. Amelia, 15, joined Maisa in the crowd outside the school gates and held a sign reading, "Our address should not decide our future". She said she was demonstrating to demand the same rights as students elsewhere in the country.       "The education authority is not investing enough in the suburbs. It's classist and racist," she said.  Ulysse Rabate, a political scientist at Paris 8 University, said the protests show the way that France's marginalised urban neighbourhoods are increasingly influencing national politics. "When there is a collapse of the public service, of public education, those who feel it the most, and the most violently, are those at bottom," he said.

A French firefighter extinguishes a fire on the street amid clashes between protesters and police during a high school students protest in Pantin near Paris as part of nationwide protests to demand the hiring of substitute teachers, increased resources and better learning conditions, as more than 400 schools remain closed following days of student protests that have escalated into violence in some places, France, Oct 2, 2026. (Photo: REUTERS/Tom Nicholson)

POLITICAL FLASHPOINT The nationwide demonstrations and blockades , which began last week, have become a political flashpoint at a sensitive moment for the government, which announced a series of deeply unpopular spending cuts in its 2027 budget on Thursday. The education budget is set to increase by a below-inflation 1.7 per cent to €65.53 billion, excluding teacher pensions. The education ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Education Minister Edouard Geffray said that education remained a priority and the below-inflation budget increase was due to population decline. The protests started in the Parisian suburbs, where poverty levels are high, then spread to Paris itself and other French towns, including Marseille, Strasbourg, Tours and Lille.  At Lycee Le Corbusier, classes including maths, humanities, English and sport have been canceled since the start of the academic year due to a teacher shortage, according to Karima Kara Ali, an elected parent representative.  In Seine-Saint-Denis, two-thirds of high schools took part in protests on Thursday, the CGT labour union said. Youth, teachers and parents in four towns complained of unsanitary school conditions and chronic staff shortages including of nurses and social workers.  Louise Paternoster, a representative for the Seine-Saint-Denis branch of the CGT's education union, said the area does not get adequate resources for its student population and their educational needs. Two-thirds of schools in the department have unfilled teacher positions, according to a union survey.

A student carries a barrier in front of a banner which reads "equal opportunities" suspended on the front of Louis-le-Grand high school in central Paris, on Oct 2, 2026. (Photo: AFP/Simon Wohlfahrt)

NOT ENOUGH TEACHERS "Our students are losing out on study time. Some schools don't have drinking water. We are not equal to other departments," she said, blaming shortages on government cuts of 3,256 teacher positions nationwide in 2026. In Pantin, a town on the northeastern edge of Paris, teacher Dilan Roche joined her students as they protested outside their school this week to support their demands and protect them from the police. "What they wrote on banners, we wrote in a letter to the local education authority: overcrowded classes, no nurses, no social workers - which is problematic for students with learning difficulties, many living in precarity," she said. While France ranks in the middle of OECD countries for spending on education, the average expenditure per secondary school student has remained little changed over the last decade, standing at €11,660 in 2024 and €11,910 in 2010, according to education ministry data.  The last nationwide high school protest movement on this scale demanding more funding came in the 1990s. That followed the government sharply expanding access to the baccalauréat, the school-leaving exam that typically paves the way to university, without providing schools with sufficient additional resources, said Professor Clemence Cardon-Quint at Paul Valery University, who researches education funding.  The movement won an increase in funding, but spending per student later stagnated despite growing demands on schools. Cardon-Quint said students and teachers have taken on additional responsibilities over the years, including navigating Parcoursup, the university admissions system introduced in 2018 and criticised by some students and teachers as opaque and discriminatory. "In a period of budgetary restraint, it is more difficult to reduce inequalities," said Cardon-Quint.

Source: Reuters/ec
